utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. May we hear the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, with Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we start with today's witness, I wanted to announce that we will have a 65 ter (i) meeting today at 3.00 in my office. May I ask, then, the usher, please, to escort the witness into the courtroom. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Dakic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: All the participants, and also you, Ms. Dakic, had time to think over that what was said yesterday under your testimony. And before I ask you, as I did on several occasions in the past, whether when rethinking that what you have said yourself, whether or not there should be some clarification and maybe some correction, I have to give you a two-fold admonition. One thing is that whatever might have been wrong in the past in this case, this could never amount to a case where this Tribunal has jurisdiction. However, even though there might be an answer which tends to incriminate you yourself, you have the right not to answer this concrete question. And by doing so, and sticking to the truth, you do not run any risk to be subject to any kind of investigation here in The Hague. However, if the Prosecution should have good cause to believe that in part your witness may be not the truth or proprio motu, this Chamber may act under Rule 91. What is Rule 91? It's the consequences which may result from a failure to tell the truth as you yesterday solemnly declared. And you should only be aware - at this moment I don't want to go into procedural details - that the maximum penalty for false declaration under solemn declaration shall be a fine of 100.000 euros, or a term of imprisonment of seven years, or both. This is Rule 91 paragraph (g), sentence 1. So when we continue the line of questions, please be aware of this. May I ask you, as a learned lawyer, did you understand this admonition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I then ask you, when reflecting about that what was discussed yesterday, do you believe that you have to add something, to correct something from that what was your testimony of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to add. I have nothing to correct either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then let me go into some detail again. Questioned by the Court: [ Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To repeat again, you told that us you were not present when the request by the Defence arrived to provide the Defence with a documentation on the health condition of one of our witnesses. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as that request is concerned, first somebody from the Defence team came and inquired as to how he could make a request to obtain something for the purpose of a trial before this Tribunal. I told that representative that everything that needs to be sent to somebody has to be decided first by the chief administrative officer of the health centre. Then the Defence addressed the CEO, and at that moment, there was no longer a need for somebody to ask me anything. And I've already told you - I told you yesterday - that this was not the first request of such nature sent to the health centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was this person who, in the beginning, approached you, as you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Predrag Radulovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And to the best of my recollection, you told us when the actual request arrived, you were not present. But it was discussed with you, or at least shown to you, this request. Can you please tell us who signed this request?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This request had a stamp of the lawyer's office, and I did not read the request carefully because what was in the request or in the letter was that Mr. Stakic's Defence wanted to obtain documents regarding the health condition of a certain person. And my job consisted of the following: That request was later on forwarded to the department that has all these documents at their disposal. Those documents are not at my disposal; those documents are at the disposal of the department that deals with the health protection of the employees. And when that documentation was located, I never inspected the medical file of that person because the file is all in codes, codes are entered by the doctors. When they do that, they follow a certain nomenclature prescribed by the Minister of Health, and that is something I really do not understand, so that's why I didn't inspect those documents carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And later on, those documents were sent to the Defence. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was it accompanied by a letter?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't draft any letter, nor did anybody tell me to draft one. Whether there was somebody else, a secretary or somebody else, who wrote a letter to accompany that documentation, I really can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If we would try to find these documents, where could we find them? Is it in one of your files?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes; everything that we receive or send should be filed, should be in the archive or on the files of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My question was concrete: Is it in one of your files, in responsible --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unless somebody has destroyed it. It does happen sometimes that things go missing from the files; however, any destruction of documents from the files is punishable by law and subject to a certain procedure, investigative procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have never been in Prijedor, but please tell me, is it correct that when this request arrived, it arrived -- or did it arrive in Prijedor or did it arrive in the unit in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing arrives in Omarska. Whatever bears the address of the health centre stays in the post office until the moment the person that is in charge of collecting the mail goes to the post office and picks up everything that bears the address of the health centre and brings it to the health centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And who did the search within the health centre on this documentation?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A paramedic in the occupational medicine department. Who was it who was put in charge of locating this particular file amongst several thousands of other files in the -- amongst the documentation, I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it is and it stays your testimony that you in person, being responsible for legal aid in this health facility, that you, before sending this documentation to the Defence, were never asked whether or not this would be in line with the law.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in that sense, not in the sense whether this is in line with the law. I've already explained to you why was it that we thought when we were approached by the Defence team for Dr. Stakic that it was our duty to deliver such documentation to this Tribunal. A year or so before that, SFOR came to our institution and told us that they needed some documents that would serve the purpose of this Tribunal. I was not present at that time. The person who was present was Zdravko Salabalija, the head technician. SFOR then took some documents from the health centre. Along those lines, I thought, and so did my superior, when the Defence team approached us, we thought that to serve the truth and to serve justice, we were supposed to deliver the requested documents. We have never denied such a request if we had one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you are aware that when there is a request implemented by SFOR, this request is always accompanied by a search and seizure order edited or issued by a judge. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any such document because I wasn't there on that day, but I suppose that SFOR did have a court order for the seizure of those particular documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let -- before we conclude this part, yesterday the Prosecution tendered two articles, 13 and 14, of the law on protection of health of Republika Srpska. I understand that it's tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May I have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We're not tendering it, for reasons I'd rather explain in the 65 ter conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then may I hear submissions by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we talk about this issue, I think that we should have in front of us the law on cooperation with the Tribunal of Republika Srpska from which actually we got the power to ask for such a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is a different issue, and we don't want to discuss it here because there is actually no case about this. But it's just a question to admit into evidence Article 13 and Section 14, Article 98, paragraph 5 - that's the part that is translated - into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would like to discuss this in the 65 ter meeting, as the Prosecution proposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. The admittance into evidence can only happen in open Court. Therefore, admitted into evidence as J -- what would be the next number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: J25. Then late in the evening yesterday, you were confronted with a number of documents, a number of lists containing names. Leaving aside for a moment the formal question whether these lists have to be signed or not signed, for the persons where we can read the names and where we know that they are either on the list of missing persons or we know that they have been killed or we only know about their fate on the basis of a maybe DNA analysis, isn't it true that when you worked at that time in the health centre, you were aware that one after the other, the Muslim doctors - you said not only, but most of them Muslim doctors - disappeared?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that they were disappearing. Actually, I never knew what was going on with them, whether they had gone away or whether they had been brought in to the investigation centre. One could never obtain any information. I was not the one who could obtain that information. The only thing I knew at the time was that people stopped coming to work, or I stopped seeing people in town. Where those people were at the time, I was not in the position to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And yesterday you told us, and it's easy to follow your line of thoughts, that everybody knew everybody in Prijedor, in this relatively small town. And is it really true that you want to tell us that you didn't know about the fate of these persons, about the doctors you knew extremely well in your own health centre?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't know all the doctors in the medical centre. There were over 1200 people working in the medical centre at the time and it was impossible to know them. There were rumours circulating about people being arrested. I heard around those days that somebody called Kiki was killed. When the Dayton accords were signed and when everything was over in the territory of Prijedor Municipality, some two or three years ago, again, I learned that the same gentleman called Kiki was alive. As for the information that somebody was either arrested or killed or moved away, that information could never be a hundred per cent correct or true. I was not in a position to be able to know with a hundred per cent certainty the names of the people who were taken to this place or to another place or who went this way or another way. It was impossible for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. me to know. There were all sorts of rumours, but one couldn't believe them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So to be, once again, quite concrete, you were never involved in the concrete dismissal of personnel of the health centre Dr. Mladen Stojanovic in Prijedor in one, all, or some of the units connected with this health centre?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During 1992 and 1993, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And once again, you never saw these lists?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in detail. I never looked through those lists. But they were available for you to look at in the personnel services. That particular section did have insight into those lists, but it wouldn't have been fair for me to go there, use my access there, and look through those lists. It would have been inconceivable for me to go and see the head of the health centre and ask him to see the lists. I did not have the authority to do so. I may have seen them if they were just on someone's -- lying on someone's table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In this period of time, there was no doubt a shortage, as we learned from several witnesses, related to the necessary medicine and, in addition, medical assistance, because it was wartime and there was an extreme pressure. We know that a number of people returned back from the war, from Croatia, they came to Prijedor. We had a number of incidents causing extreme harm to persons from all sides involved in these incidents. Wasn't it necessary immediately to find replacement for these doctors no longer available for the health centre?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Replacements, no, no replacements were requested at that time. During -- in the course of 1992, 1993, and 1994, very few doctors arrived. In 1993 and 1994, when the municipalities of Petrovac, Kljuc, Drvar, Grahovo, Livno, and all those municipalities of Western Krajina fell, the population kept withdrawing, and the doctors who were working in those institutions came with them. And when they came to Prijedor Municipality, to Banja Luka, to Gradiska or any other town in Republika Srpska, they would report medical institutions. And wherever they decided to settle eventually, managers of those health institutions would usually allow them to join. Some of them are still working at those institutions. Where exactly, well, that very much depended on where they settled themselves or where their family went. Some of them later went to other places; and in the meantime, we have young doctors straight from med school who came to work at the health centre or in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Were you, in 1992, involved in at least the attempt to fill those gaps when doctors left, were dismissed, or disappeared?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A final issue: Yesterday, you expressed yourself that from the view of today and the retrospective, it is also for you extremely difficult to understand why all this happened in Prijedor. From your point of view as a citizen of Prijedor, and as you stated, everybody knew everything about the other one, you knew a number of persons - you mentioned concrete names - who do you think yourself is responsible for that what happened in 1992 in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult for me, with my knowledge and my information, to say who was responsible. However, everything that had gone on before the end of April and May 1992, and here I'm referring to the struggle of the Muslim and Croatian peoples for Bosnia and Herzegovina and to secede from the former Yugoslavia, as well as the desire of the Serbian population to remain in the former Yugoslavia, a state in which in addition to Serbs, you also had Macedonians, Montenegrins, Hungarians, the Albanians in Kosovo, and many other ethnic groups. So probably this striving of the Muslim and Croatian peoples to secede is probably what caused everything that later happened. This one person or the persons who would have been responsible for what happened, I don't think I could name a single person or any specific persons. For me to point my finger at someone in particular and say he or she is responsible, I would need to have a lot more information than I do. The way I see things, though, everything began when my Croat and Muslim neighbours expressed their desire to -- for Bosnia and Herzegovina to secede from the former Yugoslavia. The way I see things, that is where it all started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt it's your right to see this from this angle. But to be more concrete on that what happened in Prijedor, when did you for the first time learn that camps or investigation centres were set up?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard, perhaps in late May, immediately after the combat operations that took place in Prijedor Municipality after the 22nd of May. I would pass by Keraterm and I saw people standing outside, within the perimeter. At the gate, I saw members of their families who would bring them clothing or something else perhaps. I never came close enough to have a proper look. I never approached the gate. There was a war, so it wasn't usual or normal for you to just walk around asking questions whatever you wanted to know about. I heard, and I knew when I came to the Omarska health station, that at the iron ore mine at Omarska, there was a hall in which people were being kept, people who, as I understood at that time, had been arrested either during combat operations or while they were in the areas where -- when all the areas where combat operations were ongoing were taking place, and that was all I could learn at that time. As I told you before, the police officers providing security for the people being kept in those facilities spoke to us and came to us when they needed medical assistance to be provided to whoever needed medical assistance. So both doctors and paramedics did go there. Sometimes some of those seeking medical assistance would be brought directly to the Omarska health station, usually escorted by the police, but I was never myself in any of those rooms when this happened. Now, whether this also happened on those days when I wasn't there, I should suppose that it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know Madam Minka Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you speak with her about the fate of her husband?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I did not talk to her about her husband's fate. But I did talk to her about her children's fate. I sat -- I was sitting in this room when Dr. Minka Cehajic, I think it was the end of August or perhaps September, came to see us. And we all said hello. We all greeted each other, and we asked her about her children. And she said that she used the assistance of her colleagues and workmates to evacuate her daughter, her daughter's child, and her brother to Zagreb. And she expressed an enormous debt of gratitude to the particular friend who helped her to do this. Whatever she said about her husband -- all she said about her husband on that occasion is that she wasn't sure what his fate had been. The situation was somewhat unpleasant because we were not close enough for me to ask her about such personal issues. Whether Dr. Cehajic ever told anyone else, perhaps someone that she was much closer to, anything about her husband's fate that she didn't tell us, I really couldn't know. What our conversation was about was How are you doing? and How are your children doing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mrs. Dakic, can you tell us, what is the name of the place where you lived and where Veljko Guberina's radical party was established?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Have you been present at the meeting of the party?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And how did you know that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: -- was elected as president of the board of the party? For Omarska, I presume.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was easy to find out. The meeting at which the party was founded, I could watch the whole thing from the window of my house. Many people from Omarska attended this meeting. And it's only natural that the next day, everyone knew that Mr. Stakic had been appointed president of the party's board for Omarska. Now, whether there was anything else involved, I didn't know. But all I knew was that this referred to the area of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... party was closer to you. What did you mean by saying so?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There may have been a misunderstanding due to an error in the interpretation. I was not a member of any party. When I spoke about this meeting, what I meant was the physical proximity, the meeting taking place near where I lived, that's what I meant. But I have never been a member of any political party, which includes the radical party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Excuse me. Have you seen Dr. Stakic among the participants of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't really see that clearly, because there were a lot of people there. I was perhaps a hundred or a hundred and fifty metres away from where the meeting was taking place. That's my window. I was watching from my window. I didn't really look at people's faces because you know, at that kind of distance all people tend to look alike. But two or three days earlier, we knew already that Mr. Guberina would come to Omarska and that they would have a meeting where this party would be founded. And any of us, had we chosen to do so, could have attended this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... in 1992, Muslims started to leave Prijedor. Can you explain us why Muslims started to leave Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no way for me to tell you how someone was feeling and why someone decided to leave. But there is one thing I know for a fact: Many families from the Prijedor area, even before the war, used to work in the countries of the west, starting from 1970 and then up until 1990. Why certain families, wives or children, decided to leave, I never asked them. But there was another reason. As you know, as early as 1991, there were mobilisations underway all the time of military-aged men who were supposed to go to the army. They were mobilised into the JNA forces. So they had military drills up to that point. So maybe it was also for that reason. Anyone's son or husband could have been mobilised, drafted by the JNA. So maybe that was also one of the reasons why certain citizens who were not supportive of the JNA wanted to have their relatives away, at least for a while, perhaps. So if a woman's husband worked in Germany, for example, maybe that was the reason why she wanted herself and her son to travel to Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... a Serb soldier was killed in Hambarine, and then the war started. Did you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. believe that the killing of one Serb soldier was reasonable and just cause for wide-scale use of military force against Muslim civilian population?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know about that attack, but I know that we received word that a soldier had been killed. I'm not sure if it was there in that particular place that only this one soldier got killed, or maybe there were other soldiers there, too. I really don't know. The decisions and evaluations of the military officers and the army, or what they thought was enough for them to start retaliating, I really can't talk about this because these people know. They are professionals in that particular field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Argibay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning. I have two or three questions. And I'll ask the questions, just taking into consideration your quality as a lawyer, and a civilian one. I'm not going to ask you about military things. Just tell me, in April 1992, there was a takeover of the government in Prijedor. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think this happened on the 30th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Do you think a takeover was allowed by the democratic system that was in place in Prijedor at that time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the norms of the system that was in place then and which was valid throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, we were all supposed to live together in harmony, free and safe. Now, why the takeover took place, I really can't tell you because I was not a decision-maker. I did not make those particular decisions nor did I participate in the making of those decisions, and I was never really familiar with the decisions being made. So I can't tell you anything about what caused such a decision to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I didn't ask about the cause. I asked about the system. If you have democratically elected authorities, do you think a takeover is something legal in the system?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that an elected government must stay in place and operate until there is an extraordinary round of elections and this government is changed and removed, and I'm referring here to the will of the citizens of that particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: So you would agree that the government that came into power after the takeover was an illegal government?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, it's difficult for me to speak about this, both as a citizen and as a lawyer. You know that as early as the beginning of 1992, Serb deputies were taken out from the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Assembly of Republika Srpska was founded. In the light of that, certain laws were passed and decisions were made also concerning the legality and the legitimacy. But right now, I don't think I could comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure I have understood you correctly. You said that Serb deputies were taken out from the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Who took them out?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left themselves. As far as I could follow the work of the Assembly, it was quite obvious at one point that both the Muslim and the Croatian deputies, every time an important decision would be made, kept outvoting the Serb deputies. In that situation, the Serb deputies could not secure any kind of majority when decisions were being made. And for that very reason, they could not protect the interests of the people they were representing. Bosnia and Herzegovina was a state with three constituent peoples. And you've always had Serbs, Croats, and Muslims living in Bosnia and Herzegovina, plus a number of other ethnic groups, ethnic minorities, so it was perfectly normal for the three major ethnic groups to negotiate and to pass decisions by consensus. If, on the other hand, we have a situation where the representatives of one ethnic group simply cannot find a way of reaching an agreement with the representatives of the two other ethnic groups, then probably they will start feeling threatened. And in this particular case, the Serbs were outnumbered by the representatives of the remaining two ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: If you're outnumbered in a democratic system, doesn't it mean that you are a minority?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I'm being outvoted constantly, that probably means that I represent a minority and probably also that I am not in the right. But during the Assembly's work in 1992, it was quite obvious that what we were dealing with was something quite different. Of course, it's perfectly reasonable and normal for the decision of the majority to be accepted. But if there is a law which has not received a single vote of support from any of the Serb deputies, and if there are amendments to be made, if there are further clarifications to be made, and then none of this is accepted, the same thing would have applied to also Muslim and Croat deputies. It could have been the case that a majority in the Assembly could have been constituted by the Muslim and the Serb deputies. So if that had been the case, the Croats would have been in the same situation as Serbs were in now. For a multiethnic country like ours, this is never a good situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Some moments ago, you said at page 18, line, I think, 13 or 14, that they will start feeling threatened. What kind of threats do you think they were?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. I don't understand what you're asking me to tell you. Are you referring to the Muslim ethnic group in Prijedor Municipality maybe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: No, I think you were talking about the deputies of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were not threatened personally. What was threatened was the interest of the population that elected them to the Assembly, and it is the deputies' duty to look after the interests of the people that they represent. I didn't mean that they were threatened personally, as individuals, but that under those circumstances, the interests of the people whom they represented was -- were threatened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And those interests you think were best served by leaving the Assembly and forming, say, a parallel government?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the fact that Croats and Muslims, and especially Muslims, wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina to become an independent sovereign state, and given the fact that the Serbian people wanted the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain within the former Yugoslavia, obviously these two interests clashed. They could never be the same and identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Well, you haven't answered my question, but never mind. Can you tell me, when was it that Bosnia and Herzegovina was admitted as an independent country by the United Nations? Do you remember that date?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When answering the questions by Judge Vassylenko whether and why it was just the Muslims leaving the territory even before April 1992, how is it possible that you, only one or some moments before - page 11, line 8 to 10 - you told us that probably this striving of the Muslim and Croatian peoples to secede is probably what caused everything that later happened. Is it really your testimony that those people fleeing from the territory, having caused the threat?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not just the Muslims and Croats who fled the territory. There were a number of Serbs who were leaving, a certain number of Serbs also left the territory. But I told you that I do not have enough information and knowledge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you can't change your testimony. Yesterday at 8:13 to 14, you especially stated spontaneously that it was Muslims leaving the country. As a follow-up to this answer, Judge Vassylenko put another question to you and you answered in the same direction. And may I add the following: You discussed also Trnopolje, and you told us yesterday - I have to refer to the time because my LiveNote has the wrong pagination, at 3.08.20, there was a person saying, "If you go to Trnopolje and if you are registered there, then it will be easier for us to leave the territory of Republika Srpska." Does it mean that it's your testimony that people in Trnopolje were there on their own will, that they even volunteered to go to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them. Some people whom I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever heard about --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever heard about the incidents happened to a bus leaving from Trnopolje in the direction of Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Where was that incidents -- what are you saying? Where was that incident?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you don't know about this incident, if you want to tell us that you don't know --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- don't know about these incidents, then we have to evaluate ourselves your entire testimony, going into the details of your own words. It's now for the Defence to add their questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have any questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From the side of the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Dakic, do you think Muslims would have been leaving the Prijedor area because they were fearful for their lives?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably they did, because we were all fearful for our lives and the lives of our families. In the territory of Prijedor Municipality, there were a lot of armed people at the time. Wherever there are arms around, you are never safe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you hear about an incident of a person by the name of Zoran Zigic who came to the Prijedor hospital and stabbed a patient in the chest?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that patient was of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And he simply walked out of the hospital, and he was never arrested in 1992 for committing this act?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he wasn't -- maybe he was brought in and kept for several days, but as far as I know, he wasn't. But I also know that Mr. Zigic repeated a similar act later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There are no other questions. The witness is excused. May I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Defence, the next witness would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next witness will be here at 10.30, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So maybe it's a good time to make a pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did we already discuss the issue of protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No protective measures for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps to use the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Anything you want to introduce with the assistance or during the examination as an exhibit or as evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll be maybe using one of the maps, which is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But nothing new, no surprise today?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nothing new, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, we just might use the time to ask if the Defence has the list of the witnesses for next week. And I know I'm a little confused by which witness will testify tomorrow because at one point I had asked for a switch, but at this point, the Prosecution is prepared for either one. It's up to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We follow the Prosecution request, so we switched the order, so as they asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The next one would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dragic -- number 020 is Dragic Milovan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then followed by 040. Correct? And did I understand it correctly that number 58 we can strike from the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, he is coming for the next week. Something was wrong -- his house was damaged in this harsh weather conditions in Bosnia, so he had to stay. He is coming the next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When can we expect to receive the list for next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll try to provide it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If we could just ask, if it's convenient, if that witness that was going to testify this week and testifies next week could be the first, because we already have the search completed on that witness, we've prepared it, if that's convenient. And just so it's not confused, what I understood from Mr. Lukic is now the order for the last two witnesses this week will be 47 and 40. We had asked that number 40 go last, and he indicated that he would comply with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What is your estimate about the time you need for the upcoming witness, number 30 [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we estimated it in our proffer, two to two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we take it that Witness Number 20 may be on a standby basis already for today, to start if need may be. So in the moment, the trial stays adjourned until 10.50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I ask the usher to immediately escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you for coming. May I ask, can you understand me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And may we please hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take your seat. And the witness for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dragic.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, can you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: Milovan Dragic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When were you born, Mr. Dragic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: 19 March 1953.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: In Orahovac in Gradiska Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where do you reside?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: Currently, I reside in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: I have a degree in economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the personal data that we've just heard, I would like to ask you something about the events prior to April 1992. Did you observe something unusual already in 1991? What was the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time? What I meant was whether the war in Slovenia and Croatia and mobilisation calls had any effect on Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: Obviously, the events in the environment of Prijedor Municipality had an impact on the thinking of the common people and the overall situation in Prijedor Municipality. It is well-known that at the beginning of 1991, the JNA forces in Slovenia clashed with the Territorial Defence of Slovenia, and as a result of that, Slovenia seceded from the former federation of Yugoslavia. The situation in Slovenia, obviously, had an impact on all of the republics, including Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in turn, including Prijedor Municipality. The developments of the situation in Slovenia continued in Croatia. In the Republic of Croatia, there was an armed conflict in the immediate vicinity of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, of Prijedor Municipality. Already in 1991, we had a number of refugees coming from the republics of Slovenia and Croatia into the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including Prijedor Municipality. As far as Prijedor Municipality is concerned and the attitude of its population towards the events in Croatia, the people started moving out on a large scale from Prijedor Municipality. Those were people of Croat and Muslim ethnicities. And this process intensified after the departure of the -- of JNA members to the western Slavonia theatre of war in the Republic of Croatia. The departure of the population and of -- that is, of Muslims and Croats, was by buses. There were daily departure of these people by buses. And depending on the day, there were two or three or even more buses departing Prijedor Municipality on a daily basis. If we put that into a time context, and if we bear in mind that all of that lasted for five months, between July and December 1991, we can reach a total figure of those who moved out from Prijedor Municipality. Those, again, were members of the Muslim and Croat peoples. As far as the political situation in Prijedor Municipality was concerned, one has to bear in mind that Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the end of 1990, saw the first multiparty elections. As a result of these elections, we had a new government in Prijedor Municipality which consisted of the Serb and Muslim ethnicities in the ratio of -- in the 50/50 ratio. This structure of power reflected the composition of the population according to the 1991 census. Let me briefly go back to the last three months of 1991 when the federation of Yugoslavia was still in place, and when the official army was still the JNA. The JNA started mobilising people, and men who received mobilisation papers from the JNA were sent to the front lines in Western Slavonia, in the Republic of Croatia. Serb men responded to the mobilisation calls to a larger extent, and Muslims and Croats responded in smaller numbers. However, the majority of Muslims failed to respond to mobilisation calls. The reason why they failed to respond is known only to them, but at the time, it was considered disobedience or disregard of the law of the state in which we all lived. Those people who were sent to Western Slavonia were those who responded to the mobilisation calls. Muslims, on the other hand, organised protests. Once it was in front of the municipal building. And they urged people not to respond to mobilisation calls. Obviously, this was not widely accepted by the people because any failure to respond to a mobilisation call by an official state organ constituted violation of the prevailing law as a result of which such a person who failed to respond to the call could be prosecuted by the military court. For political reasons and for the purpose of secession and creating an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, the majority of Muslims and some Croats did not respond to mobilisation calls and didn't go to the front lines in Western Slavonia. Talking about 1992 and the political situation in Prijedor Municipality, I'm referring to the first three months of the year, between the 1st of January and the 31st of March, 1992, briefly, the political situation was quite stable. As during that period, I was a member of the Executive Board of Prijedor Municipality and occupied the position of the secretary for the economy and social activities, I was very familiar with the political situation across the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you would just excuse me for a moment, I would just like to clarify something. Are you saying that the political situation was stable or unstable? And if you could then, please, continue.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: As I said, the political situation during the first three months of 1992 was unstable. And an example I can provide is Muslims who were members of the Executive Board, there was a boycott. And on a number of occasions, they openly boycotted the passing of decisions concerning the construction of an elementary school building in the Urije neighbourhood in Prijedor Municipality. The construction of this elementary school building had begun already prior to 1991. In order to continue building the school, it was necessary to -- for the Executive Board to adopt a decision. According to the ethnic makeup of the Executive Board, it had four Serb members and four Muslim members. On many occasions - I would say at least three or four times - the board failed to adopt this decision; and due to this, the elementary school building could not be finished. As for children from that particular area, they had no school to go to. They used premises in the town itself was that were rented, that were rented out to them by the secondary school for electrical engineers. This is one example I can give you of how the government failed to operate and how Muslims could not accept, or refused to accept, reality; in this case, the need for the Executive Board to pass this particular decision, and yet, it couldn't be. Nevertheless, in the beginning of April 1992, the Executive Board did adopt such a decision simply because one of the Muslim members -- following guarantees and pleas on our part, there was a vote, and the Muslim member voted in favour of the Serb proposal. So the result was five against three in favour of the decision, and the decision could finally be adopted. However, what seemed noteworthy was that the same man, the Muslim member of the board, was suspended from work the very next morning. The reason was precisely that he voted the same as the Serb members of the board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. No doubt in 1992, this was interesting for you and your special work. But could Defence please Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. explain what is the relevance for our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance we found in the fourth amended indictment, all through the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You have before you the testimony of the witness related to school buildings, one party not understanding, the other understanding. And what has this to do with the allegations in the fourth amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Even you, Your Honour, asked today about the takeover of power. We think that we should explain why the power has been taken over. This gentleman was a member of the Executive Board of Prijedor Municipality. He took part in political affairs, political happenings in the Prijedor Municipality prior to the takeover, so we think that he can explain what the political situation was in Prijedor Municipality at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: General, of course, but I think we shouldn't go into details of problems of the secondary school and problems related to this but concentrate on the questions on the relationship as indicated in the proffer between the -- as you stated, the executive and the powers of the Municipal Assembly. I think we can't go into any details of that what happened in Prijedor at that time with each and every building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This gentleman - your earphones were off at that time - explained what happened to the member of the SDA who tried to cooperate. That member was replaced tomorrow by the SDA; suspended. So we think that it is very relevant in which way SDA was acting at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I follow the transcript carefully. Please concentrate on the relevant questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Bodies of the executive power, do you think they functioned well or badly at that time? The secretariats which were held by members of the SDA, did they operate willfully and in disregard of decisions adopted by the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: Throughout that period - to specify, I mean the period starting with the 1st of January, 1992, until the end of April 1992 - to put it briefly, executive power did not function. What I said in my previous answer, the executive power was divided between members of the Serb ethnic group and the Muslim ethnic group, and the division was roughly 50/50, or four against four in terms of numbers. I can give you a good number of examples where certain secretariats were not functioning, were not implementing the decisions of the Executive Board. And I'm talking about secretariats led by Muslims. Obviously, they had received instructions from somewhere else, probably from their political patrons or, more specifically, from the leaders of their political party, the SDA. So it seemed that political decisions were more binding for them than the decisions adopted by their own institution, the institution for which they worked. And I am referring to decisions taken by the Executive Board. So there was a lot of willful activity and behaviour, and even violations of the existing laws in their work. If needed, I can also specify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I would be interested whether it's just speculation or you have any kind of evidence that there was a systematical obstruction from the side of the Muslims, as you just wanted to state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to name an example, there was a decision by the Executive Board that no new people should be recruited and employed by certain secretariats because this was not envisaged by the internal organisation of work and tasks for administrative organs. The municipal administration for social income, or as they call it today, the tax revenue office, led at that time by Meho Tursic, a Muslim, he was hiring new employees on behalf of his office, which means that he was acting in disregard of conclusions adopted by the Executive Board. To add insult to injury, the very people they hired were not adequately qualified for the tasks that they were hired to carry out. Neither did their -- nor did their qualifications respond to the requirements set out in the documents envisaging the internal organisation of those services. Furthermore, the secretariat for urban planning, housing, and communal services and property matters, there were also violations of the existing laws. There was also refusal to comply with decisions taken by the Executive Board. These violations and this disregard were reflected in the fact that land owned by the town was given to Muslims, that decisions were made for certain pieces of land owned by the town itself to be given to Muslims, despite the fact that the relevant laws, laws which were also valid before the war and that are again valid today after the Dayton accords, when land owned by the town is awarded to natural or legal persons, such land can only be allocated by the Municipal Assembly, and not by any single individual or a member of any of the institutions. These two examples can be documented, provided that the documents have been preserved in Prijedor Municipality. These two examples demonstrate that some members of the Executive Board and some government organs led by Muslims violated the provisions of the then relevant laws and acted in blatant disregard of the decisions adopted by the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the takeover on the 30th of April, 1992, which position did you occupy at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: Following the takeover, after the 30th of April, 1992, I held the post of head of communal services, which was a body of municipal administration. The main activity of that particular office is the construction of housing facilities and business premises in -- across Prijedor Municipality. Another task was the maintenance of local roads, the implementation of a programme of shared expenditure pertaining to the urban sector of the municipality, the management of state-owned apartments, and all apartments were state-owned. Prijedor, as a municipality, had about 5.600 flats at that time, or apartment units. And the organisation, the institution, which I led was in charge of investing into the maintenance of these facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the takeover on the 30th of April, 1992, what was the situation like and what happened at the end of May or in the second half of May?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: If we look at the political situation in Prijedor Municipality, or if you look at the political party in power, I told you before already that the organs of government were not exactly functioning, and I backed my statement with a number of valid arguments. The chief reason for another government to be set up which would start functioning was that the republican organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time had sent an order through their own organs, more specifically, through the Ministry of the Interior, to attack the military facilities and barracks in Prijedor, to confiscate the military equipment, and to block the roads around Prijedor. That order was sent through the Prijedor branch of the Ministry of the Interior, and the order was signed by the then Minister of the Interior personally, Mr. Alija Delimustafic. The summary of this decision would be an attack against Serbs. After the takeover, and it was a nonviolent takeover, without a single bullet being fired, without anyone getting injured or even killed - and I'm here referring to non-Serbs - a new government was set up in Prijedor including Serbs. The main organ of that government was still the Executive Board with its administrative organs and with its secretariats which had been established by the law on state administration which was then in place. In May, there were open attacks against Serbs. What form did these attacks take? There was an armed attack on the military barracks in Prijedor. There were murders of Serbs. If I remember correctly, the first murder occurred at the very beginning of May. I think the victim's name was Dzapa, and he was shot from the back. Likewise, in the village of Hambarine, an armed attack was carried out on a car carrying members of both the Serb and the Croat ethnic groups. And it was on that occasion, if I remember correctly, that two persons were killed and two persons were seriously wounded. In the town of Prijedor itself, the situation was rather tense. The tension culminated in late May when there was an organised, armed attack on Prijedor. The attack came from various directions. During the attack, some 15 army members were killed. Likewise, there were a number of wounded army members. Some houses were destroyed and fire was set to others, all of which resulted in considerable damage. So much about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how and for how long did Kozarac prepare for these conflicts? What can you tell us about that? And also, what was happening in Kozarac before the takeover, when military convoys were passing through it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: A very interesting piece of information about the local community of Kozarac in Prijedor Municipality would be this: This local community had between 18.000 and 20.000 inhabitants in the community itself and the neighbouring villages which belonged to that local community. In late 1991, journalists and representatives of the foreign media came to Prijedor. The president of the Executive Board organised a press conference, which I attended. After that, we saw a videoclip featuring the population of Kozarac local commune preparing themselves for an armed rebellion. I don't know who the author of that videoclip is, but it is interesting because it lasts for about three hours and it features all the details of the preparations for an armed rebellion. Obviously, having watched that videoclip, all those who attended the press conference and who saw this for the first time were struck by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. panic. They simply couldn't believe that something like that was happening in the immediate vicinity of the place where they found themselves at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I interrupt at this point in time. We have to take the break now. We, the three of us, we reviewed both the proffer and the transcript where the Defence indicate the reason why to call this witness, and now we're discussing issues not foreseen there. And we regard it necessary to be prepared in order to follow the testimony of the witness. The trial, therefore, stays adjourned until 12.30. --- Break taken at 11.56 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The witness may be brought in immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Maybe, Your Honour, before the witness comes in, you asked me where in our proffer you can find my last question, and I asked about military convoys which were passing through the Kozarac. And it's the last sentence of the proffer, stating that: "The armed Muslims with automatic rifles, machine-guns, and other armaments blocked the JNA convoy and threatened the same." So the fact is the witness gave a lengthy answer, but we should be a little bit patient and let him explain the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We come back to this this afternoon. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dragic, I asked you about a military convoy, one or more of them, that passed through Kozarac before the war and the situation in Kozarac before the takeover and the outbreak of the armed conflict. You told us that you had seen a videoclip featuring all that. Can you please explain what you saw on the videoclip and can you also tell us about your experience with the passing of military convoys through Kozarac before the armed conflict started.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: I have told you that all those who had the opportunity to see this videoclip, lasting for about 180 minutes, that all those who saw this videoclip were astonished when they saw how many Green Beret members there were, and the arms they had in their possession. They were also astonished with the organisation of their work. It was clear to everybody that what they saw was an organised unit which had military discipline, implying that members of that military formation would line up every morning. All of us who were watching this were immediately reminded of the times when we had to serve military service, the compulsory military service in the JNA. Obviously, one could also see a number of familiar faces in that videoclip, which the participants of the press conference found very surprising. We couldn't believe that those people that we all knew and associated with changed sides overnight, so to say, and became members of the Green Berets, and that their objective was to prepare an armed rebellion against the Serbian population. I had an opportunity to see such formations personally from a close distance. Once, when I was returning from Banja Luka, I was riding in an official car. There was a roadblock on the road between Banja Luka and Prijedor in Kozarac. I saw a convoy of military vehicles carrying military equipment that was pulled over at the crossroads where the road forks off towards Kozarac. That was the main road between Prijedor and Banja Luka. So we couldn't proceed towards Banja Luka via that section, and we could only take a bypass through Kozarac in order to reach Prijedor. As we were driving on this bypass road, we passed by the Muslim cemetery there. I saw a number of Green Beret members lying on the ground with automatic weapons in their hands. That was in the cemetery. As we were passing by the cemetery, we were stopped by some of the Green Berets, and there were three or four cars in front of the car that I was driving in. The column of cars was stopped, and it was pulled over. But shortly after that, we were able to continue travelling on that bypass road. When I finally arrived in Prijedor, and when I got to my office, I told my colleagues the story of my journey from Banja Luka, and what I had seen. I could see that they were quite surprised to hear all that, and that they were also scared. They simply couldn't believe that such armed formations with such weapons really existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, when did you come across this roadblock in Kozarac? Can you be more specific about the time when this happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the time of in the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No; when was it in terms of the calendar time? Can you please stop just for a ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, you are fine? Otherwise we could have a break, if you need a replacement. Okay. Thank you. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, can you specify the time frame for that event.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact date, but it was in the month of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were a member of the Executive Board of Prijedor Municipality prior to the takeover, which means while the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor was Mr. Cehajic. Did you ever see Mr. Cehajic give any orders to the army? Did he have the authority to issue orders to the army?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: Of course, as a member of the Executive Board of Prijedor Municipality, I knew the president of the Assembly of Prijedor Municipality, Mr. Muhamed Cehajic. I am not aware that Muhamed Cehajic gave any orders to the army, because he had no legal authority to do so. But in connection with your question, I do remember one event that was much debated in the town at that time. Mr. Cehajic, together with the president of his party, Mirza Mujadzic, and there was a third gentleman with them, Medunjanin - I forgot his first name - the three of them went to meet the officials in charge of the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks in Prijedor, the military officials in charge of the barracks. During that meeting, or at least that's what people said, they demanded that mobilisation papers not be sent to Muslims, and they told the military officials that unless their demand was complied with, they would organise mass rallies of Muslims outside the municipal building in Prijedor, as well as outside the barracks, the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks in Prijedor. It's easy to conclude that the demand made by the delegation at the barracks was illegal and unconstitutional, if you look at the laws and the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that point, the law on national defence. And yet, they considered themselves entitled to make such a demand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the president of the Executive Board during the time that you were a member of the Executive Board of Prijedor Municipality, do you know whether the president ever gave any orders to the army?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: While I was working as the secretary for the economy and social activities as part of the Executive Board of Prijedor Municipality, had any such order or decision ever been sent to members of the army, I would have known of it. But during my service as the secretary, no such request, no such demand was made by the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard or seen the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor give any orders to the police?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: During the time I was occupying the position, my position in the Executive Board of Prijedor Municipality, I was not aware of the president of the Executive Board ever sending any orders to members of the police. And I am sure that no such orders were ever given because that would have been illegal and unconstitutional. He would not have the authority over the work of the police, whereas other bodies did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The president of the Municipal Assembly, according to the laws in place at that time, could he give any orders -- was he in position to give any orders to the police, and were you ever aware -- did you ever hear of Mr. Cehajic giving any orders to the police?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: The president of the Assembly, Mr. Cehajic, Muhamed Cehajic, while I was working as the secretary, to my knowledge he never ordered the police to do anything because, again, as we've already said, he was not legally entitled to do so. He did not have the authority. And anyway, the police would not have carried out his orders simply because the president of the Assembly did not have the legal authority to issue orders to the police. More specifically, speaking of the public security station, the police station in Prijedor, the police were given their orders by the security centre in Banja Luka or the Ministry of the Interior based in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragic, in 1992 [sic], you were mobilised yourself. Excuse me, I said 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So in 1991, you were mobilised and sent to Western Slavonia. During your stay on the front lines, did it ever happen that a municipal civilian organ of authority gave you any orders?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: In 1991, sometime in late August and early September, I was still working as the secretary for the economy and social activities in Prijedor Municipality. And in this period, I received a military call-up from the Yugoslav People's Army. Naturally, at that time, the JNA was the only legal and constitutional armed force of the state I was living in. I responded to the call-up. I went to the front in Western Slavonia, and I worked there as a communications officer at the command of the 43rd Brigade of the JNA. We were far from the front line itself. I spent about 45 days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you the following: During those 45 days in Western Slavonia, did it ever happen that a municipal organ of civilian authority or a municipal politician, for that matter, ever came to your command, to your headquarters, and give you any orders, or did any written order ever arrive there?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: As I've said a moment ago, I was in Western Slavonia, or more specifically, at Bijele Stijene, for about 45 days. During my time there, no oral or written order from the civilian authorities in Prijedor was received. Had I ever received one, I would have considered it ridiculous due, simply, to the fact that I was a member of the JNA units there. According to the former Yugoslavia's constitution, and according to the relevant laws, including the law on national defence, the JNA was independent in making its decisions and no orders or decisions could have been handed down to the JNA by any level of civilian authority, and nothing like that ever happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The civilian authorities in Prijedor, after fighting broke out, did the civilian authorities complain that too many people were in the army and that, therefore, it was not possible to go about the daily civilian tasks in the proper way? Could the civilian authorities issue an order to have a number of civilians released from the army?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: Certainly. When someone went to the JNA to join one of the units, it was the civilian sector, or the civilian authority, that was at a loss. They were losing people to the army who were in certain civilian positions, doing civilian jobs prior to being drafted by the JNA. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Regardless of that, regardless of the fact that when people left from the civilian authorities to join one of the JNA units, the civilian authorities were facing a shortage of work force, and regardless of this, the civilian authorities could not do anything about it. The civilian authorities could not do anything to bring those civilians back from the front line or from the JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to having the right to mobilise people, did the army also have the right to mobilise equipment or materiels without receiving approval from the civilian authorities? And which were the bodies through which the army mobilised both people and equipment? Can you tell us that.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: The organs of military authority, according to the law on national defence, if there was a mobilisation, if men were being mobilised, or if manpower was being mobilised, as the military usually call it, the national -- the law on national defence entitled them to carry out this mobilisation. And they were also entitled to commandeer equipment. When I say "equipment" or "materiel," I am referring to means of transportation, equipment and technical equipment, even animals used to draw the equipment. I mean horses in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know through which organ, through which body exactly, the army mobilised people and equipment?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: The army, or the different bodies of the army, mobilised people and equipment at municipal level through the secretariat for national defence. Those were municipal organs for one period of time; and during a different period of time, they were republican organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the secretariat for national defence was a municipal body, did it receive its orders from the municipal authorities or from the republican secretariat for national defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: This secretariat, as I've said, was, for a certain amount of time, a municipal body. And then in different period, it was a republican body. In both cases, this body did not receive orders from civilian authorities. They could only receive orders from the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During this trial, we have heard that sometimes police units were being sent to the front. The Minister of the Interior, did he have the authority to send his people to the front, or was this also done by the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: Talking about the police, if you look at the way the police is organised, they had their regular forces and their reserve forces. According to the law, the reserve police forces are only used under exceptional circumstances, in exceptional situations. As far as the specific question is concerned, if you look at the reserve forces of the police, the decision to send reserve forces into war-torn areas could only be made by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Following the takeover on the 30th of April, 1992, you have told us already which post you held. Can you please be so kind as to tell us which body of the municipal authority did you report to and who did you report to? Who did you go to between the 30th of April and the 30th of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of my testimony, I said that the institution of which I was the head was a municipal administrative organisation. As such, it answered to the Executive Board of Prijedor Municipality; or more specifically, to the president of the Executive Board. According to the book of rules governing the work of the Executive Board, administrative bodies and municipal administrative organisations sent reports on their work to the president of the Executive Board of the municipality. This report on their activities would be sent twice during a year, a calendar year, for two distinct periods of time. The first period was from the 1st of January to the 30th of June, and the second period was from the 1st of July to the 31st of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever submit a report to the Crisis Staff, or did you receive any order from the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Were you aware of the existence of the Crisis Staff, and how did you perceive that body?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
utterances.text: As for the first part of your question, I've already told you that the institution that I headed had its own book of rules and reported twice a year to the Executive Board and to the Executive Board only. When I was discharging these duties during the given period of time, I heard of the establishment of a Crisis Staff in Prijedor Municipality but I didn't know who its members were or where it was physically located, where it was physically headquartered. Throughout the entire 1992, because of the nature of my duties, I was in the building of Prijedor Municipality every day. I attended consultations with the president of the Executive Board as well as with the secretaries of the respective administrative bodies. The need for daily consultations and cooperation with members of the Executive Board reflected in the fact that the institution that I was the head of had, at the time, one of the most important duties that the civilian authorities in any municipality usually discharge. Because of the nature of the activities of my institution, I had to have daily contacts with the president of the Executive Board and its members. As I said at the beginning of my testimony, I heard of the existence of the Crisis Staff, but while I was discharging these duties - and that was up to January 1993 - I didn't notice anything that would reveal to me the existence of that body, of that Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Kindly give us the names of the members of the Executive Board with whom you had frequent contacts.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC
